title: Shaved hazel walking stick
subtitle: A drawknife-finished stick from a straight hazel stem
excerpt: A walking stick in green hazel: a straight coppice stem, bark removed, drawknife-shaved to a smooth taper, and finished with danish oil. Hazel produces long, straight, naturally tapered sticks with very little waste. A beginner's first shaving-horse project.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.
A managed woodland system where trees are cut to the stump on a rotation, producing multiple straight stems from each stool. Hazel is the most common coppiced species in Britain.
A foot-operated clamp bench for holding work while using a drawknife or spokeshave.

content.text: Hazel from a coppice stool produces straight stems 1.2 to 1.5 m long with a natural taper from root to tip, which is exactly the taper needed for a walking stick. The stem is cut in winter, bark removed at the
shaving horse
while in the
green wood

state, and dried straight before finishing. A beginner project because hazel is the most cooperative green-woodwork species: soft under the drawknife, consistent grain, and the natural form does most of the design work.
Before you start cutting.
Drawknife: the drawknife is pulled toward the body. Control the bevel angle and the stopping point. Never allow the blade to travel past the thigh.
Shaving horse: the foot pedal must lock the work before the drawknife stroke begins. If the work moves, stop and reset.
Workspace: stable ground underfoot. Loose or uneven footing under the shaving horse is a hazard with drawknife work.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Wood
Hazel from a managed
coppice

stool, cut in winter (November to February), ideally five to seven years old from the stool. At this age the stem is 2 to 4 cm at the base and 1.2 to 1.5 cm at the tip over a 1.3 m length. Hazel straightens as it dries and is easy to correct during drying by tying to a straight rod. Ash or sweet chestnut are good alternatives from the same coppice system.
Method
Step 1: Select and cut the stem

Select a straight stem with minimal side branches. Cut at the stool, leaving 15 to 20 cm of stub to protect the stool and allow re-growth. Cut the top just above a bud. Clean off any small side shoots with a sharp knife while the stem is still fresh.
Step 2: Remove the bark at the shaving horse

Mount the stem in the shaving horse with the thick end away from you. Use the drawknife with the bevel down for bark removal: the bevel-down position takes thin, flat shavings of bark rather than digging into the wood beneath. Work from the thick end to the tip in long, even strokes.
Green hazel bark comes off cleanly in one season after cutting. If the bark has dried and hardened (more than six weeks after cutting), soak the stem in water for twenty minutes before working.
Step 3: Even the taper

After bark removal, check the taper. Some stems have slight bulges from side-branch nodes. Use the drawknife to remove these high spots, working with short strokes just over the node, blending it into the taper on each side.
Step 4: Dry the stick straight

Dry the stick suspended horizontally in a shed or garage for six to eight weeks. If the stick starts to curve, tie it gently to a straight rod with cotton tape and re-check weekly. Hazel dries within two to three months in a dry, ventilated space.
Finishing

Once fully dry, apply danish oil with a cloth. One coat, left twenty minutes, wiped surplus. Two coats total over two days. Cure for five to seven days before use. The danish oil protects the clean hazel surface and brings out the pale honey colour of the dried wood. A rubber ferrule (walking-stick tip) is fitted to the base before use.
Variations
Burn a decorative band around the stick at the handle end using a pyrography tip before finishing.
Source a stem where the root flares naturally to form a grip. The root end of a hazel coppice shoot often has a slight natural hook at the stool.
Leave the bark on and apply danish oil directly over it for a darker, more rustic look. The bark on dried hazel is stable and adheres well.

attrs.cause: The stem had inherent tension from its growth position (the outer arc of a bend or a stem from a shaded position).
attrs.fix: Tie the stick to a straight rod with cotton tape, checking the bend weekly. Hazel corrects readily if tied within the first two weeks of drying.

attrs.symptom: The drawknife is digging into the wood beneath the bark
attrs.cause: The bevel angle is too steep (bevel up instead of bevel down) for bark-removal work.
attrs.fix: Flip the drawknife to bevel-down for bark removal. Bevel-up digs deeper and is used for shaping, not for stripping bark.
